title: Electrochemical Reduction of CO2 on Flame Annealed Cu
abstract: Surface modification of metallic Cu by conventional oxidation and an alternative method of oxidation using flame annealing and its influence on electrochemical reduction (ECR) of CO2 are reported in this study. The ECR of CO2 in aqueous KCl electrolyte yielded methane, ethane, ethylene, and hydrogen as the major products. The faradaic efficiency of ethane obtained at 1.2 V vs NHE for flame-annealed Cu (34%) was comparable to the conventionally oxidised Cu (40%), while bare Cu yielded methane (10%). The metal–metal oxide interface on the electrode aids in the formation of C2-based products. Flame annealing can be regarded as an alternative electrode preparation method for C2 product formation, with its merits in high specific surface area, self-rejuvenating mode on deactivation and ease of preparation.

sections.heading: Electrochemical Reduction of CO2 on Flame Annealed Cu
sections.text:
Gopalram Keerthiga*[b] and Raghuram Chetty[a]
Surface modification of metallic Cu by conventional oxidation and an alternative method of oxidation using flame annealing and its influence on electrochemical reduction (ECR) of CO2 are reported in this study. The ECR of CO2 in aqueous KCl electrolyte yielded methane, ethane, ethylene, and hydrogen as the major products. The faradaic efficiency of ethane obtained at 1.2 V vs NHE for flame-annealed Cu (34%) was comparable to the conventionally oxidised Cu (40%), while bare Cu yielded methane (10%). The metal–metal oxide interface on the electrode aids in the formation of C2-based products. Flame annealing can be regarded as an alternative electrode preparation method for C2 product formation, with its merits in high specific surface area, self-rejuvenating mode on deactivation and ease of preparation.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
Flourishing interest in catalysis for CO2 valorisation demands a stable and selective electrode for its commercialisation. Feasible use of CO2 to a higher carbon product yields highenergy-density liquid fuel. It has abundant applications as an alternative source of carbon.[1–4] Several authors investigated the electrochemical reduction (ECR) of CO2 in a variety of metallic, bimetallic, and metal-oxide electrodes.[5–8] Among them, Cu, a medium hydrogen overvoltage metal, has attracted considerable interest because it yields hydrocarbons as the major product.[9] Further development of the Cu catalyst is aimed at improving stability, selectivity and activity criteria by varying either the electronic effect or the geometric effect.[10] Experimental[11] and theoretical[7,8] studies revealed tailoring metal through surface activation,[12] alloying,[13,14] oxidation[3,15] and electrodeposition[16] offers an effective way to improve CO2-to-hydrocarbon conversion. Recently, Guo et al.
[17] reported a hierarchical nanoporous ellipsoidal catalyst derived from a nanoscale metal-organic framework with micropores and interconnected mesopores benefitting the electroreduction of CO2 by enhancing the CO2 concentration and accelerating the mass transfer process. In another study, a new strategy for the design of CO2 electrolysis systems with better economic viability was reported by a combined electrolysis system integrating CO2 reduction with the chlor-alkali process. [18]
Surface modification of Cu through oxide film formation is catalytically selective in converting CO2 to C2 products, wherein
heat treatment of metal offers a possible route to disrupt catalyst deactivation by reducing overpotential.[19,20] In situ fragmentation of Cu2O nanoparticles has been reported to enhance the C C coupling and suppress the hydrogen evolution reaction while reducing CO2.
[21] Au/CeOx and Cu/SnOx nanoparticles supported on CNTs offer strong metal-support interaction for targeted electrochemical CO2 reduction. Sn electrodes with an oxide layer grown on them offer increased faradaic efficiency (FE) and current density for formic acid compared to untreated (etched) Sn electrodes.[22] Density functional theory calculations correlate the enhanced catalytic activity of oxide-derived Sn electrodes to the promotion of surface hydroxyl groups favouring higher hydrocarbons.[23,24]
Raciti et al. demonstrated CO2 reduction on Cu nanowires obtained after annealing, and subsequent reduction promotes distinct surface structures and improves CO selectivity.[25] In air, annealing Cu foil yielded CO and formic acid at a lower reduction overpotential,[3] while the electrodeposition of thin and thick Cu2O film yielded ethylene and ethane, respectively. Frese et al.[26] performed CO2 reduction on an intentionally oxidised Cu electrode, illustrating that the Cu/Cu oxide electrodes promote CO2 reduction. Mazare et al.
[27] attempted to reap a maximum photoelectrochemical response by comparative evaluation of flame-annealed and furnace-annealed ordered TiO2 nanotubes.
Flame annealing is a highly suitable method for preparing a well-ordered electrode where the surface carbon impurities and organic molecules are removed during fast quenching.[28] Attard et al.[28] were instrumental in employing flame annealing to control surface sites and reconstruct the Pt single crystal electrode for the oxygen reduction reaction. The electrode’s enhanced performance is attributed to the enlarged active surface area and an increased number of reactive species in a short time compared to a long cooling period in conventionaloven oxidation.[28] Flame-annealed FeO nanoparticles on stainless steel felt offered higher current density for a microbial bioelectrochemical system because of its strong chemical stability, its conductivity, and its large specific surface area.[29]
By contrast, the fabrication of oxide film by thermal oxidation needs an optimal time, temperature, and annealing atmos-

In situ attenuated total reflectance infrared (ATR-IR) spectroelectrochemistry studies on metastable oxides of Pb, Bi, Sn and In were reported by Pander et al., who classified the materials as oxide active (In and Sn), oxide buffered (Pb) and oxide independent (Bi) electrodes for CO2 reduction. [30] Guo et al.[31] reported a maximum formic acid FE of 30% for heat treatment of Cu by electropolishing and annealing.
Dedicated research on metal oxides for CO2 reduction focuses on optimising oxide formation parameters, thereby controlling the composition of suboxide formed. Li et al. concluded oxides are reduced to metal during reduction, resulting in CO2 reduction efficiency.
[3] Yeo’s group reported an CH3 mediated pathway for ethane and ethanol formation on thick and thin copper-oxide-derived Cu catalysts.[7]
Flame annealing results in clean, cheap and well-ordered electrode surfaces;[27] and breaks down the passive layer,[29] thus ensuring a high specific surface area for ECR of CO2. Hence, its comparative evaluation with bare and conventional oxidised electrodes helps appreciate its behaviour towards ECR of CO2 reduction. Herein, we have investigated oxidised Cu electrodes obtained by two different methods-namely, conventionally oxidised Cu (referred to as OC Cu) performed for 2 h at varying temperatures (200–1000 °C) and a quick flame-annealed Cu (referred to as FA Cu) prepared by exposing Cu to a Bunsen burner for 2 min-and evaluated their catalytic activity towards CO2 reduction in KCl electrolyte.

sections.heading: Results and Discussion
sections.text:
Figure 1 shows the X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns for bare Cu, OC Cu and FA Cu electrodes. Pure Cu electrodes showed reflections corresponding to the (111), (200) and (220) planes.[32] For OC Cu and FA Cu electrodes, a slight shift in the major Cu planes was observed, possibly due to the internal stress developed by the thermal expansion of oxide.[33] In Figure 1, additional reflections at 36.6° (111), 42.4° (200) and 61.2° (220)
correspond to Cu2O, and 32.8° (110) corresponds to CuO. [34,35] The additional reflections increase with the oxidation temperature for the conventionally oxidised electrodes, as shown in Figure S1.
Figure 2 shows the scanning electron microscope (SEM) images of oxidised electrodes. Micrographs of the conventionally oxidised Cu showed pillar-like cubes (Figure 2A), and flameannealed Cu showed uneven humps (Figure 2B) compared with bare Cu, where the insets in Figure 2 show the higher magnification images of the same. With a gradual increase in temperature, the morphology and composition of Cu vary from particulates with an orientation of pyramid (800 °C) to disintegrated structures (1000 °C) for the conventionally oxidised electrode, as shown in Table 1 and Figure S2.
Figure 1. XRD patterns of the bare and oxidised copper electrode. * indicates Cu2O and # indicates CuO.
Figure 2. (A) SEM images of conventional oxidised Cu (OC Cu). Inset in the figure shows a magnified image of OC Cu. (B) SEM images of flame annealed Cu (FA Cu). Inset in the figure shows a magnified image of FA Cu.

Figure 3 shows the high-resolution X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) Cu 2p spectra of bare Cu and oxidised Cu electrodes. Bare Cu electrodes showed spin-orbit doublets of Cu 2p core level transition at 932.7 eV (Cu2p3/2) and 952.5 eV (Cu2p1/2), respectively. [36] The oxidised electrodes showed satellite peaks at 939.8 and 943.6 eV.[36] Deconvolution of the Cu2p3/2 spectra into two peaks at 932.4 eV and 933.6 eV corresponds to Cu2O and CuO. Although it is challenging to distinguish Cu+ and Cu in XPS based on these two peaks, copper LMM Auger electron spectroscopy (AES) analysis can be used to confirm the coexistence and presence of Cu+ and Cu, as reported by Wang et al.[37] The percentage values estimated from the XPS plot showed 50.4% for OC Cu and 48.6% for FA Cu, indicating the predominance of the Cu(I) species.
The deconvoluted O1s peak showed a metal oxide species on the surface. The peaks at 530.5�0.1 eV, 532.5�0.1 eV and 531.3�0.1 eV correspond to Cu2O, CuO and bare Cu phases,
respectively, attributed to adsorbed oxygen or hydroxyl groups on the Cu surface (Figure 4, Table 2).[38]
The determination of thickness and surface roughness of the oxide layer was inferred from Li and Kannan.[3] The averaged energy dispersive X-ray (EDX) composition of the oxidised surface (Table 1) aids in the estimation of the Cu :O ratio. The thickness and Cu :O ratio increased with the temperature for the conventionally oxidised Cu, except at 1000 °C, where a passive oxide layer was formed. Flame-annealed Cu showed an oxide thickness of 8.1 μm and a Cu :O ratio of 80 :20 (wt.%). Identical composition and thickness were observed for the conventionally oxidised Cu at 500 °C for 2 h. The roughness of the oxidised electrode increased with the temperature of oxidation (Figure S3, Table 3). However, the decrease in surface roughness of FA Cu could be due to the removal of surface impurities during the flame annealing. Hence, the results for OC Cu (500 °C for 2 h) and FA Cu are compared for CO2 reduction ability in the following section.
The current potential curves were performed in an H-type cell on a 1 cm2 electrode with N2-saturated KCl solution as a control and compared with the CO2-saturated solution shown in Figure 5A. With the change in potential, a double-layer region develops, and the successive oxidation (I)/reduction (II) peaks were observed due to the difference in the transition of valence states of copper (i. e. Cu, Cu I and Cu II).[39]
The increase in current density near peak III ( 1.1 V vs. normal hydrogen electrode [NHE]) can be attributed to both the hydrogen evolution from aqueous electrolytes and the reduction of Cu oxides in the absence of CO2.
[39] The peak IV for FA Cu showed an increase in current density at potentials greater than 0.7 V vs. NHE for the CO2-saturated solution (24 mAcm 2) in comparison with that of the nitrogen-saturated solution (∼10 mAcm 2), signifying the interaction of the electrode with CO2 and its subsequent reduction. A comparison of the CO2-saturated cyclic voltammograms of FA Cu and OC Cu with bare Cu (shown in Figure 5B) indicates the oxidised electrodes offer higher cathodic current, implying an increased reduction of CO2.Figure 3. Electrolysis of the CO2-saturated solution in an H-type cell with the oxidised electrodes followed by its headspace analysis revealed methane, ethane, ethylene and hydrogen as the major products (Figure S4). Over a time of 4 h, FA Cu yields average methane of 34 μmolcm 2, ethane of 161.5 μmolcm 2, ethylene of 53.7 μmolcm 2 and hydrogen of 45 mmolcm 2 compared to the conventionally oxidised Cu, which showed average ethane of 395.5 μmolcm 2, ethylene of 197.7 μmolcm 2 and hydrogen of 24 mmolcm 2 (Figure S5). The electrodes oxidised at 200 °C, 800 °C and 1000 °C showed varying C2 (ethane and ethylene) products (Figure S5) based on Cu :O ratio and surface roughness.[40] However, with the increase in oxidation temperature, C2 (ethane and ethylene) formation reached a plateau with the increase in the thickness of the electrode (Figure S6), emphasising that the thickness of the oxide layer governs the product formation rate.[3]
In the literature, the selectivity of oxide-derived copper towards C2 products has been attributed to several factors, such as (i) a higher local pH at the catalyst surface, favouring the C C coupling pathway over the formation of C1 product; [41] (ii) more grain boundaries, defect sites and crystal planes; and (iii) the presence of oxides, which provide Cu sites with multiple valences to increase the catalytic activity.[37,42,43,44] Eilert et al. reported the existence of subsurface oxygen during CO2 reduction-enhanced C2 selectivity because of changes in the electronic structure of the Cu, improving the binding of CO.[45]
Furthermore, the selectivity for C2 products depends on the higher surface roughness, leading to increased local current density and the mode of CO2 adsorption during the reduction.[46,47] C2 formation on OC Cu and FA Cu can be ascribed to the high surface roughness of the annealed Cu (as seen in Table 3) and higher electrochemically active surface area.[41]
Stability measurements performed for 3 h showed an initial reduction of Cu oxides followed by constant current density, as illustrated in Figure S7. The characterisation by XRD (Figure S8) and SEM (Figure S9) of the oxidised Cu samples before and after CO2 reduction depicts the reduction of oxides to the metal in par with the literature results,[3] and a newly formed Cu surface helps in C2 formation. [7]
Figure 6A shows the FEs as a function of FA Cu potential where ethane, ethylene and methane with a maximum FE of 34%, 17% and 22%, respectively. Comparison of FA Cu and OC Cu (Figure 6B) at 1.2 V vs. NHE showed similar FE for ethane (OC Cu: 40%, FA Cu: 34%), ethylene (OC Cu: 20%, FA Cu: 17%) and hydrogen (OC Cu: 33%, FA Cu: 36%). Consequently, CO2 reduction on bare Cu electrodes yielded maximum FE for methane (43%) at 1.6 V vs. NHE, which is 0.4 V higher than the maximum FE obtained on oxidised Cu electrodes. Lower overpotential of CO2 ( 1.2 V vs. NHE) on oxidised Cu electrodes attributes to the properties of metallic Cu0 electrodes resulting from the reduction of the oxide layer,[3] while the enhanced C2 product formation on oxidised Cu could be due to the formation of active sites at the metal-oxide interface.[20]
To illustrate the role of the metal-oxide interface, the oxidised Cu electrodes were compared with commercial Cu, CuO and Cu2O powders. The powder was pelletised, fabricated as electrodes and studied for CO2 reduction at 1.2 V vs. NHE. As seen in Figure 7, the sequence of methane formation follows metallic Cu (72 μmolcm 2)>Cu2O powder (38 μmolcm
2) > FA Cu (25 μmolcm 2)>CuO powder (18 μmol cm 2) > OC Cu (16 μmolcm 2)>Cu powder (8 μmolcm 2), and the inset in Figure 7 depicts maximum ethane formation of 239 μmolcm 2 and 328 μmolcm 2 for FA Cu and OC Cu, respectively, in addition to comparable ethylene formation. These findings showcase the need for a metal-metal oxide interface with definite crystal planes for the facile formation of C2 products. [20]

Table S1 summarises the products formed on the FA Cu and OC Cu with some of the literature reported on oxide-derived copper by thermal annealing, electrochemical oxidation and anodisation.[6] The products formed at similar reduction potential, and the FE was comparable to the reported work.[42,46,47]
Research on the relationship between Cu surface structure and product composition demands a comprehensive understanding. Flame annealing of Cu electrodes results in a clean diffusion-enhancing surface and a thinner catalyst (8.1 μm), minimising mass transport limitations.[4] It burns off the adventitious carbon deposit and offers clean electrochemically active sites for reduction.[29] Flame oxidised stainless steel felt was reported to be a good alternative to the conventional carbon-based electrodes to enhance the current output in bioelectrochemical systems.[29]
For selective ECR to C2 products, optimisation of thickness and Cu :O ratio tunes the product formation. The role of metal oxide interaction (Figure 6) and the influence of thickness (Figure S6) towards CO2 reduction were established. A comparison of the XRD reflections of the oxidised Cu electrode before and after CO2 reduction shows the disappearance of Cu2O (111) peaks (Figure S8), which may be attributed to in situ reduction of Cu (I) sites during CO2 reduction, as reported in the literature.[3] A unique understanding has been derived for flame-annealed Cu for ECR of CO2, where further insights from theoretical and mechanistic studies are in progress.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text:
The oxidised Cu electrode was studied for CO2 reduction by conventional oxidation of Cu, which involves varying the treatment temperature and time in a tubular furnace. In this work, an alternative, low-cost and simple approach to oxidise Cu electrodes was developed via quick exposure to a Bunsen
burner flame. FEs of 40% for ethane and 33% for hydrogen were observed on OC Cu electrodes, compared to efficiencies of 34% for ethane and 36% for hydrogen on FA Cu, at a potential of 1.2 V vs. NHE. The maximum FE of the C2 product was achieved for oxidised electrodes at lower overpotential compared to the products formed on bare Cu electrodes.[29]
This study verifies the reduction behaviour of FA Cu and OC Cu for ECR of CO2 is not profoundly different. Because of its low cost, easily scalable mode of preparation and FE comparable to OC Cu, flame annealing can be considered an alternative electrode preparation method for the oxidation of copper towards ECR of CO2.
Supporting Information Summary
The supporting information contains the detailed experimental procedure to obtain the electrodes and their characterisation. Comparative table of faradaic efficiencies on various oxidized Cu electrodes for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 is presented. Supporting XRD patterns, SEM images, cyclic voltammetry, chronoamperometry, and electrolysis experiment graphs are also provided.
